title: Role taxonomy, resource hierarchy, and tenant-scoped permissions matrix for RBAC v2
creator: Aisha Kapoor
description:
Goal: Design RBAC v2 role model that supports resource hierarchy, tenant-scoped roles, fine-grained scopes, and a permission matrix that is compatible with Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.

Scope:
- Define canonical resource hierarchy (organization > workspace > project > model > deployment > artifact).
- Define scope primitives (read, write, admin, manage-billing, manage-keys, deploy, view-logs).
- Produce a permission matrix mapping actions (API endpoints, console routes, admin hooks) to scope primitives and roles.
- Specify inheritance semantics, exceptions, and overrides for tenant and cross-tenant delegation.
- Outline migration path from RBAC v1 (coarse role buckets) to v2 while preserving compatibility for existing tokens and API keys.
- Integrate audit logging requirements per write/admin actions and map them to the platform auditing pipeline.
- Surface SSO/SAML group mapping and SCIM provisioning considerations for role assignment automation.

Non-goals:
- Implementing the policy engine itself (separate task).
- UI mockups for the console role editor (will be follow-up ticket).

Background + rationale:
Current RBAC model is coarse (org-admin, dev, viewer) and does not cover resource-scoped operations required by Dedicated/Private customers or advanced internal needs (separation of duty for billing vs infra ops, least-privilege deployments, per-model inference billing visibility). RBAC v2 aims to give teams explicit primitives and stable inheritance rules so policies are predictable across deployment types, and so audit logs clearly attribute privileged operations for compliance.

Key requirements:
- Predictable inheritance: child resources inherit parent roles unless an explicit deny/override is applied.
- Least privilege-by-default: new roles default to no elevated permissions.
- Role composition: support composite roles made of scope primitives to avoid explosion of roles.
- Tenant isolation: roles must be assignable at org or workspace scope and must not accidentally grant cross-tenant access.
- Emergency access: a break-glass mechanism with time-limited elevation and explicit audit trail.
- SSO mapping: allow mapping of SAML groups to roles and support group-to-role sync (SCIM) with conflict resolution rules.
- Audit hooking: every mutation to role assignments, policy changes, or admin actions must emit structured audit events (actor, action, resource, before/after, request_id, trace_id, SSO attributes).

Deliverables:
- Canonical resource hierarchy document (CSV + yaml examples).
- Permission matrix CSV (action -> scope -> implied scopes -> recommended role composition).
- Migration plan (scripts for migrating org-level roles, token compatibility layer).
- RFC describing inheritance/override semantics and break-glass design.

Risks & trade-offs considered:
- Policy engine vs static matrix: A dynamic policy language (CEL/XACML-like) gives more flexibility but increases complexity for engineers and auditors. We recommend a primarily matrix-driven model with a small policy expression escape hatch for edge cases.
- Tag-based scoping vs fixed hierarchy: Tags enable ad-hoc scoping but complicate auditability and SLO expectations. We prefer a fixed hierarchy for core resources and optional tag-scopes as an advanced feature behind a feature flag.
- Back-compat: preserving existing API keys may allow broader access than intended. Migration will require a compatibility mode and an automated migration script followed by a 30-day audit window.

Acceptance criteria (high level):
- Permission matrix published and reviewed by Security + Platform + PM.
- RFC approved and merged to docs.
- Migration plan validated in staging with a test org.
- Audit hooks defined and sample audit events emitted for major admin actions.
- SSO mapping spec reviewed with SSO team and validated against one enterprise customer test SCIM payload.

Notes on console UX and developer ergonomics (informational):
- Console should show effective permissions (computed) and the inheritance chain on any resource page.
- SDKs should expose a permissions introspection endpoint to surface whether a token is allowed to perform an action before attempting a write (helps prevent costly retries).
- Role descriptions must be human-readable and include a link to the permission matrix row to reduce confusion.
updates: 2026-03-05: Kickoff - scoped feature and aligned on hierarchy draft (org > workspace > project > model > deployment). Attendees: Aisha, Miguel, Priya Rao (PM), Ben Collins (Security).
2026-03-07: Security review sync - decided on matrix-first approach with policy escape hatch; flagged tag-scoping as future RFC. Action: Miguel to produce permission matrix draft.
2026-03-09: Design review - trade-offs discussed: break-glass implementation (time-limited elevation + audit) accepted; draft RFC updated with break-glass flow diagrams.

2026-03-11: Staging experiment - emitted sample audit events for role assignment mutations. Observed missing request_id in one downstream pipeline; added dependency for logging-team to ensure request_id propagation (see dependencies).

decisions: Matrix-first: prefer a human-reviewable permission matrix with a restricted policy expression escape hatch.
Fixed resource hierarchy for core resources; optional tag-scopes behind feature flag.
Support tenant-scoped roles with explicit deny/override semantics; inheritance flows downward by default.
Break-glass will be time-limited, audited, and require a 2nd approver for cross-tenant elevation.
acceptance_criteria: Permission matrix reviewed and accepted by Security and Platform leads.
RFC merged to docs and signoffs recorded in Confluence.
Migration script prototype can convert RBAC v1 org roles to v2 in staging without losing admin access.
Sample audit events for role changes are visible in logging pipeline with request_id and trace_id.
SSO/SCIM mapping validated against a customer test payload and documented mapping rules.
